# Text

Body and supporting text at a named role from the type scale.

```tsx
import { Text } from "@rata/react";
```

| | |
|---|---|
| Registry name | `text` |
| Family | content |
| Tier | free |
| Status (css / react / figma) | latest / latest / future |
| Depends on | — |

## Behavior

A `<p>` or a `<span>` set to one named role of the type scale. No primitive and no state.

- **Headings are a different component** — A heading enters the document outline and is a navigation target; body text is neither. That is a difference in semantics rather than in looks, which is this system's test for splitting a component — the same test that separated Tabs from SegmentedControl. A single `as="h2"` prop here could not require a level only when the element happens to be a heading, and a heading without a level is the bug both components exist to prevent.
- **`as` offers `p` and `span` and nothing else** — Those are the two things running text is: a block of prose, or a run inside one. `div` is the one that would turn this into a layout wrapper — and a `<div>` holding text is how a component like this stops being about type and starts being about boxes. A text block that must contain block content is not one paragraph and should not pretend to be.
- **`tone` is part of it, even though the type roles carry no colour** — The type scale is size, weight and line-height only, so a caller styling text still has to pick a foreground — and picking wrongly is this system's most common token error, which `internal/vibe-tests` exists to measure. Three named steps that map onto the three documented and contrast-verified `theme.fg.*` values make the correct choice the shortest one. It is deliberately not open-ended: a role colour or a status colour on running text is a different decision, and Notice owns it.
- **`code` is not a role here** — `type.code` exists, but inline code is a `<code>` ELEMENT — a semantic claim about the content, not a size. Offering it as a role would mean either rendering the wrong element or accepting `as="code" role="code"`, which says the same thing twice. Inline code belongs to a base layer styling `code` directly, which `@rata/css` does not ship yet and which is a separate gap from this component.
- **No line clamping in this version** — `-webkit-line-clamp` is the only way to truncate at a line count and it needs three coupled declarations plus a fixed display mode, which changes how the element lays out — and truncated text needs its full value reachable some other way or the content is simply gone. It deserves its own pass rather than riding along with the scale.

## Props

Extends `Omit<HTMLAttributes<HTMLElement>, "role">`.

| Prop | Type | Default | Summary |
|---|---|---|---|
| `children` | `ReactNode` | — | The text. |
| `as?` | `TextElement` | `"p"` | Whether this is a block of text or a run inside one. |
| `role?` | `TextRole` | `"body"` | Which step of the scale this text is set at. |
| `tone?` | `TextTone` | `"primary"` | Which of the three documented foreground steps it takes. |
| `className?` | `string` | — | Extra classes, for placement — not for restyling it. |

### `children`

```ts
children: ReactNode
```

The text.

**Use when**

- A paragraph, a sentence of help text, an eyebrow label.

**Don't use for**

- Block content inside `as="p"`. A paragraph cannot contain a list or another paragraph, and the browser will silently close it early.

**Accessibility** Plain content. Nothing here is announced as anything but text, which is the point.

### `as`

```ts
as?: TextElement = "p"
```

Whether this is a block of text or a run inside one.

**Use when**

- `span` for text inside a sentence, a row or a control's label area.

**Don't use for**

- `span` for a paragraph. It is not a block, so the page's spacing rules will not apply to it.

**Accessibility** Neither element carries a role, so this changes nothing that is announced — it changes what the text is, structurally, for spacing and for selection.

### `role`

```ts
role?: TextRole = "body"
```

Which step of the scale this text is set at.

**Use when**

- `supporting` for help text under a field, a timestamp, secondary metadata in a row.
- `large` for a standfirst — one paragraph introducing a page, set above body size.
- `label` for an uppercase eyebrow over a section or a group of fields.

**Don't use for**

- `supporting` to mean disabled. It is smaller, not dimmer, and it is still meant to be read — `tone` is the prop that changes emphasis.

**Accessibility** `label` renders uppercase through `text-transform`, so the text stays lowercase in the accessibility tree and a screen reader does not spell it out letter by letter. Typing it in capitals would.

### `tone`

```ts
tone?: TextTone = "primary"
```

Which of the three documented foreground steps it takes.

**Use when**

- `secondary` for text that supports the primary content and is still read in full.
- `muted` for the least prominent text on a surface — a placeholder-like hint, a disabled row's caption.

**Don't use for**

- A status or accent colour. Those belong to a role, and running text carrying one reads as a link or an error; Notice is the component for a coloured message.
- `muted` for anything load-bearing. It is the lowest of the three and the first to fail on an unusual background.

**Accessibility** All three are contrast-verified against canvas, surface and subtle. None of them is below the text floor — this prop cannot make text fail contrast on a documented background, which is why it is a closed set of three rather than a colour.

### `className`

```ts
className?: string
```

Extra classes, for placement — not for restyling it.

**Use when**

- The margin or measure the page wants, neither of which this component owns.

**Don't use for**

- Overriding size or colour. Those are `role` and `tone`, and a hand-written value drifts from the scale the moment the seed moves.

## Use cases

### A standfirst under a page title

One paragraph introducing a page, set above body size so it reads as the way in rather than as the first paragraph of the content.

```tsx
<Text role="large" tone="secondary">Every value in this system comes from a token, and every token says what it is for.</Text>
```

`secondary` rather than `primary`: it supports the title above it and is still read in full. One of these per page — a second stops being an introduction.

### Help text under a field

A line of guidance that belongs to the control above it.

```tsx
<Text role="supporting" tone="muted">Used for billing receipts only.</Text>
```

`supporting` is smaller, not dimmer — `tone` is what changes emphasis, and the two are separate so help text can be small and still fully legible. If the field is a TextField, its own `description` prop already does this and wires up the `aria-describedby`; reach for this only outside one.

### An eyebrow over a group

A short uppercase label naming a group of fields or a section of a settings page.

```tsx
<Text role="label" tone="secondary">Notifications</Text>
```

The capitals come from `text-transform`, so the text stays lowercase in the accessibility tree. Typed in capitals it may be spelled out letter by letter. This is also the right answer when a `<Heading>` was tempting but nothing navigates to the label.

### A run inside a sentence

Part of a line needs a different step or tone from the rest of it.

```tsx
<Text>Last synced <Text as="span" tone="muted">four minutes ago</Text>.</Text>
```

`span` because it is not a block — a nested `p` would close the outer one early and the page's spacing rules would apply to something that is half a sentence.

### Reaching for the wrong component

The message is a warning the reader has to act on.

```tsx
<Text tone="secondary">Your trial ends in three days.</Text>
```

Don't lean on this and then colour it — `tone` is deliberately closed to three neutral steps, because a status colour on running text reads as a link or an error. A message that needs a colour needs Notice, which has the role tokens, the icon and somewhere to put the action.

## Real usage in this repo

```tsx
<Text>Choose which events send you an email.</Text>
```

## Token recipe

### base

One type role and one foreground step. No box: text has no padding, no background and no margin of its own.

| Property | Token |
|---|---|
| font-size | `the chosen role's size — type.body.size, type.large.size, type.supporting.size or type.label.size` |
| font-weight | `that same role's weight` |
| line-height | `that same role's line-height` |
| margin | `space.0 — the page owns the space between blocks, for the reason Heading's contract gives` |

### label

The label role carries two things the others do not, and they come from the scale rather than from here.

| Property | Token |
|---|---|
| text-transform | `type.label.text-transform` |
| letter-spacing | `type.label.letter-spacing — uppercase text needs the extra tracking to stay readable, which is why that step exists` |

### tone

The three documented foreground steps for text, and the reason this prop exists at all: it is the shortest path to the right colour, so nobody reaches for a palette token.

| Property | Token |
|---|---|
| primary | `theme.fg.primary` |
| secondary | `theme.fg.secondary` |
| muted | `theme.fg.muted` |
| all three | `contrast-verified against theme.bg.canvas, theme.bg.surface and theme.bg.subtle — see the contrast page` |
